How Nebraska property tax works

Property tax in Nebraska is handled county by county. Each of the state's 93 counties has an assessor who values property, and the Department of Revenue's Property Assessment Division oversees the work. Counties, cities, school districts, community colleges and other local bodies each levy their own tax, and the county treasurer mails the tax statements in December.

If you plan to sell, three things decide how the tax affects you: the day the tax becomes a lien, the days each half goes delinquent, and how the credits printed on the statement are handled at closing. The dates below cover all three.

Tax stepDate or rule
Valuation notice mailedOn or before June 1, to the owner of record as of May 20, when the value changed from last year (77-1315)
Taxes dueDecember 31 after the levy; a first lien on the real property from that date (77-203)
First half delinquentMay 1, or April 1 in counties over 100,000 people (77-204)
Second half delinquentSeptember 1, or August 1 in counties over 100,000 people (77-204)
Tax saleUnpaid property may be sold on or after the first Monday of March following delinquency (77-1801)

Your valuation notice and the protest window

The county assessor has to mail a notice by June 1 for every taxable parcel whose assessed value changed from the year before. It goes to whoever owned the parcel on May 20. Under section 77-1315 the notice carries a "KNOW YOUR RIGHTS" statement in the largest type on the page. That statement tells the owner that a protest can be filed with the county clerk on or before June 30, and that the parcel's value will not be certified to the taxing subdivisions until August 20.

That gap between the notice and certification is your window to challenge the number before it turns into a bill. The notice also shows when the county board of equalization convenes and the filing dates. When the assessment roll is finished and the notices are out, the assessor publishes a certification in a local newspaper that includes the last day to file protests.

Because the notice follows the owner of record on May 20, a spring closing date decides who receives it. If you sell in April or May, tell the buyer to watch the mail, and forward anything you get after closing.

Homes versus farmland

Most real property is valued at its actual value, but agricultural and horticultural land is its own class. Section 77-201 sets the agricultural rate at seventy-five percent of actual value, dropping to fifty percent for school district taxes that repay bonds voters approved on or after January 1, 2022. Land with special valuation is taxed at seventy-five percent of that special value, with the same fifty percent exception for those bonds. Property that qualifies for historic rehabilitation valuation follows a separate set of rules in sections 77-1385 to 77-1394.

This matters for a rural house on acreage. A parcel that mixes a dwelling with cropland or pasture can carry more than one valuation basis, so the tax bill will not track the sale price in a simple way. Ask the assessor which parts of the parcel are classed as agricultural before you compare your bill with a neighbor's.

What credits show up on the statement?

Under LB 34, passed in the 2024 special session, the school district property tax credit is applied directly on the property tax statement. You no longer claim it on your income tax return. The credit for community college property taxes paid is different: it is still claimed on the Nebraska income tax return using Form PTC.

The credits appear as a reduction after the full taxes levied. Credit rates are certified each fall by executive order to the State Treasurer and county officials, so the amount on your statement can change from one year to the next.

The Department of Revenue also runs a Nebraska Property Tax Look-up Tool that shows the school district and community college taxes paid on a parcel. A seller can use it to confirm what was paid before the closing date.

Who claims the credit when a house sells mid-year?

The person who paid the tax to the county treasurer claims the credit. The person who ends up bearing the cost through a closing adjustment does not. Tax counts as paid on the day the treasurer receives it.

The Department of Revenue's FAQ walks through a sale in which the seller paid all of one year's property taxes to the Douglas County Treasurer the following year. At closing the buyer reimbursed the seller for that earlier year's tax. The seller still claims the community college credit on that year's income tax return, because the money went to the treasurer before closing. The reimbursement on the closing statement does not shift the credit to the buyer.

In the same example the buyer paid part of the next year's taxes, but the treasurer did not receive that money until the year after. The buyer had paid none of the earlier year's tax to the treasurer, so the buyer had no credit to claim for it.

Keep the treasurer's receipt and the closing statement together in one folder when you prepare your return.

Owner filings besides the real estate bill

Nebraska has other yearly filings that sellers and landlords sometimes trip over. A personal property return and schedule is due each year on or before May 1. A report of damaged property is due on or before July 15. The valuation protest deadline is June 30. Check the Department of Revenue's news page each year for notices about the homestead exemption.

The personal property return is a separate filing from the real property bill, so a landlord or small business owner should treat the two as separate tasks.

If a house has storm or fire damage, ask the county assessor whether the damaged property report applies and whether the value was adjusted. A buyer who takes a damaged house as-is will probably ask the same question.

Selling with taxes owed

Taxes follow the lien, not the owner. Real property taxes are a first lien from December 31 of the levy year, so an unpaid bill stays with the house when title changes hands. The title company will check with the county treasurer on the status of each year before closing.

Before you accept an offer, gather these:

  • The last two real estate tax statements and proof of the payment dates.
  • This year's valuation notice, and any protest you filed.
  • The homestead exemption approval letter, if you have one. The state pays that share to the treasurer.
  • A note of any delinquent amount and the date it went delinquent.

If a bill is past due, the sale process under section 77-1801 can begin after the first Monday of March. The owner, an occupant or a lienholder keeps the right to redeem until the purchaser applies to the county treasurer for a tax deed. Paying a delinquent year out of the sale proceeds at closing clears it, so tell the buyer early about any unpaid year. A cash sale skips the lender's underwriting wait, which helps when a deadline is close.

Frequently asked questions

When are Nebraska property taxes due?

Taxes are due December 31 following the levy. Half goes delinquent on May 1 and the other half on September 1, or April 1 and August 1 in counties with more than 100,000 people.

When does the county assessor mail valuation notices?

On or before June 1, to the owner of record as of May 20, for parcels whose assessed value changed. The notice explains that a protest can be filed with the county clerk on or before June 30.

Is the school district credit on my tax bill or my income tax return?

Since LB 34 in the 2024 special session, the school district credit is printed on the property tax statement. The community college credit is claimed with Form PTC on the Nebraska income tax return.

Can a seller still claim a credit after the house sells?

Yes, if the seller paid the tax to the county treasurer. A buyer's reimbursement at closing does not change who may claim the credit for tax already paid to the treasurer.

Is farmland taxed the same as a house?

No. Agricultural and horticultural land is a separate class valued at seventy-five percent of actual value under section 77-201, with fifty percent applied to school district taxes on certain bonds approved on or after January 1, 2022.

What the Nebraska homestead exemption does

This is a property tax relief program in which the State of Nebraska pays all or part of a qualifying owner's tax bill on a home. The state reimburses counties and other local governments for the revenue they lose when an exemption is approved, and it pays the county treasurer directly. If only a partial exemption is granted, the owner pays the rest.

The program targets certain groups of homeowners, and for most of them it also depends on income. It is separate from an ordinary assessment appeal, and it is separate from the creditor protection that Nebraska also calls a homestead. Both meanings matter to someone thinking about selling, so this page covers each.

For the tax program, a homestead is a house or mobile home plus up to one acre around it, occupied by a natural person who is the owner of record from January 1 through August 15 of the application year. Property held only in the name of a corporation, partnership or LLC does not qualify.

Who qualifies: the eight categories

Applicants fall into numbered categories, and each one has its own paperwork. The 2026 guide sets them out like this.

CategoryWho it coversIncome limit applies?
1Owners 65 or older before January 1 of the application yearYes
2Disabled former service members totally disabled by a non-service-connected accident or illnessYes
3Owners with a qualifying physical disabilityYes
4VMilitary service members with a 100% service-connected permanent disability, or a 100% individual unemployability ratingNo
4SQualifying surviving spouses of those service membersNo
5Paraplegic or multiple-amputee service members whose home the VA helped fund, and their surviving spousesNo
6Owners with a developmental disabilityYes
7Service members with a 100% service-connected temporary disability, and their surviving spousesNo

One warning is easy to miss: qualifying for Social Security disability does not automatically qualify someone for the Nebraska exemption. Categories 3 and 6 need a medical certification (Form 458B) in the first year. The service-connected categories need VA paperwork in the first year and again in years ending in 0 or 5.

How income changes the relief

In categories 1, 2, 3 and 6, relief shrinks on a sliding scale as household income climbs, from 100% down to 0%. The 2026 table looks at 2025 income. Household income starts with federal adjusted gross income, adds items such as untaxed Social Security or railroad retirement income, and subtracts medical and dental costs above four percent of that income.

For an owner over 65, a single filer gets 100% relief with income up to $37,000, 50% up to $46,600, and 10% up to $54,300. At $54,301 and over, relief is 0%. A married or closely related household gets 100% up to $43,400, 50% up to $55,100, and 10% up to $64,500, with 0% at $64,501 and over.

Disabled applicants use their own, somewhat higher column. A single applicant in that group gets full relief up to $41,600, and a married or closely related household gets it up to $47,700.

"Closely related" means a brother, sister or parent who is also an owner-occupant, and that person's income is counted with the applicant's. Pensions, interest and IRA withdrawals count, and so does Social Security retirement income.

If you sell or move

The exemption belongs to the owner who lives in the home between January 1 and August 15, so a sale or move inside that window can change the outcome. Several rules apply directly to sellers.

  • An applicant who files on time and then buys a different home before August 15 can ask to move the exemption. The request is an Application for Transfer, Form 458T, filed by August 15 with the assessor in the county where the new home sits.
  • Someone who gets a Notice of Rejection (Form 458R) has 30 days from receipt to file the transfer form.
  • A single applicant who dies before August 16 loses the exemption for that year, because the occupancy window was not met. A surviving spouse and minor children keep the benefit for the year of death if they live in the home, and the spouse then applies again.
  • A stay away for health reasons, such as nursing or assisted living, does not break occupancy while the owner shows an intent to return. Furnishings left in place and a home that is not sold, leased or rented support that intent.

Families who inherit or help sell a parent's house should note the last point. Once the home is rented or sold, the intent-to-return argument gets weaker. Ask the county assessor how your closing date relates to the August 15 cutoff before you sign.

Yearly deadlines

Most categories file every year, and the Department of Revenue publishes a calendar from January to December. A late application is usually refused, with three narrow exceptions for filing after June 30.

  • February: assessors mail forms to last year's applicants.
  • Before June 30: the annual filing period for Form 458 and, where required, Schedule I.
  • By July 20: a county board may extend the filing deadline on written request.
  • Mid-October: letters of partial approval or denial based on income go out.
  • December: county treasurers mail tax statements showing the exemption.

The three late-filing routes are a written county-board extension to July 20, a spouse's death during the year with a death certificate attached, and a medical condition certified by a medical practitioner on Form 458L. The second and third routes allow filing up to June 30 of the following year.

Home value too high, or application denied

Even with a qualifying income, the exemption is cut when the home's assessed value is above the county's maximum. The exempt amount drops by ten percent for each $2,500 of value over the maximum, and a home $20,000 or more over the maximum does not qualify. The department publishes certified average residential values for each county in September, and assessors send Form 458R in October and November when a reduction applies.

Rejections and denials follow separate tracks.

  • A written rejection from the county assessor can be appealed to the county board of equalization within 30 days of receiving the notice.
  • A denial from the Tax Commissioner can be challenged with a Petition for Redetermination, Form 458P, filed with the department within 30 days.
  • A homestead appeal cannot be used to argue about the home's valuation. If a high valuation threatens your exemption, the valuation protest has to be filed by June 30.

The creditor-protection homestead

Chapter 40 of the Nebraska statutes gives every natural person living in the state a homestead exempt from judgment liens and forced sale, up to $120,000 in value. Section 40-101 describes it as the dwelling house where the claimant lives, its appurtenances and the land under it. Outside a city or village the cap is 160 acres. Inside an incorporated city or village, the owner may choose up to two contiguous lots instead.

This protection has limits that matter when a house is sold under financial pressure.

  • Section 40-103 allows a forced sale to satisfy judgments on debts secured by mechanics', laborers' or vendors' liens, and on mortgages or trust deeds the claimant signed and acknowledged.
  • Under section 40-104, a married person's homestead can only be conveyed or encumbered by an instrument that both spouses sign and acknowledge. A conservator or an attorney in fact under a power of attorney may act for a spouse as the section describes.
  • Section 40-116 shields sale proceeds, up to the exemption amount, from legal process and voluntary disposition for six months after the sale. Selling one homestead does not stop the owner from selecting or buying another.

When a creditor levies on a home, the owner can ask the district court in the county where the home sits to decide whether the land is exempt and what it is worth (section 40-105). Under section 40-107, the application must be served on the judgment creditor and the officer making the levy at least ten days before the hearing.

How this fits a fast cash sale

The two homestead programs come up at different points in a sale, and neither blocks a sale on its own. The tax exemption affects what the property tax statement shows and whether a refund or correction is possible. The creditor homestead affects who must sign the deed and what happens to the proceeds.

A few checks before you accept any offer:

  • Ask the county assessor whether an exemption was granted this year, and whether your sale date falls before or after August 15.
  • If the seller is married, make sure both spouses sign and acknowledge the deed and the purchase agreement. An instrument without both signatures is a problem under the statute.
  • Have the title company pull judgment liens, mechanics' liens and mortgages, since section 40-103 leaves those debts outside the exemption.

Cash Home Buyers can make an as-is offer on a Nebraska house, and the closing company handles the deed and the lien payoffs. This page is general information, not legal advice.

Frequently asked questions

Who files the Nebraska homestead exemption application?

The owner files Form 458 with the county assessor where the home is located. For categories 1, 2, 3 and 6, Schedule I (the income statement) goes with it.

Do I have to own the home in my own name?

Owner of record is the usual rule. A surviving spouse, a buyer in possession under a land contract, a joint tenant or tenant in common, a life estate holder, and a trust beneficiary with an ownership interest also count. A home held only by an LLC, corporation or partnership does not qualify.

Can I move my exemption to a new home I buy?

Yes, in some cases. If you filed on time for the old home and became owner of a new homestead before August 15, file Form 458T with the assessor in the new home's county by August 15.

What if the assessor rejects my application?

Appeal to the county board of equalization within 30 days of the written notice. If the Tax Commissioner denies it instead, file Form 458P with the Department of Revenue within 30 days.

When is the homestead exemption application due?

Before June 30 each year, using Form 458. A county board may extend the deadline to July 20 on written request.

Estate tax or inheritance tax?

Nebraska has no estate tax. What it has is an inheritance tax, which the person who receives property pays, not the estate. County court determines it, and the county treasurer takes the payment and the required report.

Federal estate tax is a separate matter. It only applies to estates above $15,000,000 for people who die in 2026, so most Nebraska families never meet it. The state inheritance tax is the one that reaches ordinary households, and it can reach a house.

What an heir owes depends on how closely related the heir was to the person who died. Nebraska sorts heirs into three classes under statutes 77-2004, 77-2005 and 77-2006.

Inheritance tax rates by relationship

For deaths on or after January 1, 2023, close relatives pay 1%, aunts, uncles, nieces and nephews pay 11%, and everyone else pays 15%. Each heir first gets an exempt amount.

ClassWho is includedRateTaxed on amount over
Class 1Parents, grandparents, siblings, children, lineal descendants, and their spouses1%$100,000
Class 2Aunts, uncles, nieces, nephews and their lineal descendants, and their spouses11%$40,000
Class 3All other persons, including friends and non-relatives15%$25,000

The tax is measured on the clear market value of what each person receives. Court decisions annotated under the statute treat that as fair market value on the date of death, minus anything the heir paid for the property.

Class 1 also takes in a person the decedent treated as a child for at least ten years before death, along with that person's descendants. Nebraska courts have weighed factors like support, discipline, shared time and written evidence when deciding whether that relationship existed.

Who pays nothing

A surviving spouse owes nothing on what passes to them, and neither does an heir under 22 years old in any class. Under 77-2004, interests passing to a surviving spouse by will or any other route are outside the tax.

  • Anyone whose inheritance stays at or below the exempt amount for their class.
  • A person under 22 receiving an interest, whichever of the three classes applies.
  • The homestead allowance, exempt property and family maintenance allowance.
  • Bequests in trust to an in-state association for exclusively charitable purposes in Nebraska.

These exemptions decide whether selling an inherited house leaves a tax bill behind. A house going to a spouse is outside the tax. The same house going to adult children is taxed only on the value above $100,000 for each child.

How the exempt amount and rate work together

Think of each heir's share as its own calculation. Take what that person receives, subtract the exempt amount for their class, and apply the class rate to the remainder. A Class 1 heir pays 1% on value beyond $100,000, a Class 2 heir pays 11% on value beyond $40,000, and a Class 3 heir pays 15% on value beyond $25,000.

When a house is split among several heirs, each share is measured on its own against that person's exempt amount. A share that lands at or below the exempt amount produces no tax, even if the whole house is worth much more than that. This is why a house left to two or three children can come out tax-free while the same house left to one friend does not.

Deductions are listed in 77-2018.04, and the county judge determines and assesses the final amount. Use the class rates as a rough guide to the size of the issue and ask the county court for the real figure.

When the tax is due

The tax is due 12 months after the date of death. Interest runs on unpaid tax from that date at the rate in section 45-104.01.

If no proceeding to determine the tax is filed in those 12 months, a penalty of 5% per month or part of a month is added, up to 25% of the unpaid tax. Filing a probate petition or application counts as an appropriate proceeding. So does filing for a tentative payment and paying it inside the 12 months. The county court can abate the penalty for good cause.

A tentative payment helps when the house is listed or under contract but the final figure is not set. Under 77-2018.07 you apply in writing to the county court. If the county attorney does not consent, the county attorney has seven days to state a different amount, and the payment can be amended later. It covers probate and nonprobate estates, and it stops interest and penalty from building while the numbers are settled.

How the tax is determined and who files what

The county court can determine the inheritance tax inside a probate case or in a proceeding opened only for that purpose. The court itself can start it, and so can the personal representative, the county attorney, or anyone with a legal interest in the property (77-2018.01).

After tax is paid, the person who filed the proceeding sends the county treasurer a Form PCIT, the Petitioner's County Inheritance Tax Report. It is due when the court order determining the tax is entered. The form counts beneficiaries and tax paid by class and by residency, and no inheritance tax can be paid or refunded before a required report is in.

"Petitioner" is defined broadly. It can be a personal representative, a trustee, someone who filed an affidavit to transfer real property without probate, or the beneficiary of a transfer on death deed. A house passing outside probate can therefore still call for paperwork at the county.

Selling before the tax is paid

A house can be sold while the inheritance tax is still open. Selling does not erase the tax, which is figured on the value each heir received, so plan early and have the money ready.

Your route to clear title depends on how the estate is handled:

  • With a personal representative, the representative signs a deed of distribution to the heirs, who then sell. That deed is on the state's documentary stamp tax exemption list, though the later sale to a buyer is not.
  • Without probate, an heir can use the affidavit for transfer of real property if at least 30 days have gone by since death, no personal representative has been appointed or applied for, and the Nebraska real property is worth $100,000 or less on the assessment rolls after real estate taxes owed. The other heirs must sign too.
  • With a transfer on death deed, the deed is recorded and a death certificate is filed. The state exempts these deeds from the stamp tax.

Creditors can reach an affidavit successor only up to the value of what was inherited, and that claim ends three years after death or one year after distribution, whichever is later. Our Nebraska probate guide covers the court route in more detail.

Recording the deed

Each deed recorded in Nebraska needs a Real Estate Transfer Statement, Form 521, under 76-214, and the register of deeds will not record without it. When the deed follows a death, the statement can ask for the date of death and whether title changed through a transfer on death deed, joint tenancy or the end of a life estate.

The documentary stamp tax on a non-exempt sale is $3.32 per $1,000 of value for deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026. Before that it was $2.32. The estate or heirs selling the house pay it as grantor, in addition to any inheritance tax owed by individual heirs.

Heirs who would rather not carry the house through listing and repairs can ask Cash Home Buyers for an as-is cash offer. A cash sale closes without a buyer's loan approval, and the title company pays the recording charges and any taxes owed from the proceeds. This page is general information, not legal or tax advice, so confirm your own numbers with the county court or an attorney.

Frequently asked questions

Does Nebraska have an estate tax?

No. Nebraska charges an inheritance tax instead, paid by the person who receives the property. Federal estate tax applies only above $15,000,000 for 2026 deaths.

How much inheritance tax would my child owe on a Nebraska house?

A child is a Class 1 heir, so the rate is 1% on the value received above $100,000. A child whose share stays at or below $100,000 owes nothing.

Does a surviving spouse pay Nebraska inheritance tax?

No. Interests passing to a surviving spouse by will or any other means are not subject to the tax under Neb. Rev. Stat. 77-2004.

When is Nebraska inheritance tax due?

12 months after the date of death. Interest runs on unpaid tax from that date, and a penalty of 5% per month, up to 25%, can apply if no proceeding is filed in time.

Can I pay part of the tax before the final amount is set?

Yes. A tentative payment can be made after a written application to the county court, with the county attorney's consent or a court order, and it can be adjusted later.

How Nebraska treats a quitclaim deed

A quitclaim deed is an ordinary deed for recording and tax purposes in Nebraska. One rule sets it apart: if the grantor later picks up more title, that extra title does not pass to the person who took the quitclaim. The rule is in Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-209.

The statute starts from the opposite position. When a deed claims to convey more than the grantor owned, anything the grantor acquires afterward normally flows to the grantee. Quitclaim and special warranty deeds are carved out of that benefit. The Nebraska court said the same in Troxell v. Stevens (1899).

The word deed is defined broadly. Under 76-203 it covers every written instrument that creates, transfers, mortgages or assigns real estate or an interest in it, other than wills and leases of one year or less. A quitclaim fits that definition, so the usual recording and transfer statement rules apply. The state's Form 521 even has its own box for "Quit Claim", next to warranty, corrective, sheriff and transfer on death.

What the register of deeds needs before recording

The register of deeds will record a quitclaim only if it is signed and acknowledged, follows the page format rules, and arrives with a completed Form 521. Each requirement lives in a different statute, which is why people miss one.

  • Acknowledgment. Inside Nebraska, 76-217 requires the acknowledgment to be made before a judge or clerk of any court, a United States magistrate, or a notary public. An officer cannot take an acknowledgment outside his or her territorial jurisdiction.
  • Blank space. 23-1503.01 calls for a blank area at the top of the first page, at least three inches by eight and one-half inches, for the recording stamp. Without it the office may add a page and charge for it.
  • Paper and print. Pages run between 8.5 by 11 and 8.5 by 14 inches, black text on white paper of at least twenty-pound weight. A font of at least eight points is presumed legible.
  • Signatures. Use black or dark blue ink; digital or electronic signatures are allowed. Type, print or stamp each party's name under the signature.
  • Transfer statement. Under 76-214, the grantee files a completed statement when the deed is presented. Without it the register shall not record the deed.

That statement is Form 521. The deed will not be recorded unless items 1 through 27 are filled in and the grantee or an authorized representative has signed.

Recording fees and stamp tax

Recording costs $10 for the first page and $6 for each added page, under 33-109. Of that, $2.50 of the first-page fee and 50 cents of each added page go toward preserving records and modernizing the register's office. A certified copy of a recorded instrument costs $1.50 per page.

The documentary stamp tax comes on top unless an exemption applies. The current rate is $3.32 for each $1,000 of value or fraction of a thousand, as shown on the Department of Revenue's stamp tax page. Section 76-901 drops the rate to $2.32 for transfers on or after January 1, 2032.

ChargeAmount or rule

For a family quitclaim with no stated price, call the register of deeds in your county and ask whether the office applies market value or assessed value before you bring a check. Counties describe nominal-consideration transfers in different words.

Quitclaim deeds that skip the stamp tax

A quitclaim is exempt when it falls into a category in 76-902. For a house, the usual one is a transfer inside the family with no real consideration: between spouses, between ex-spouses for property acquired or held during the marriage, or between parent and child.

Other exemptions that often apply:

  • Deeds that confirm, correct, modify or supplement a recorded deed without extending or limiting the existing interest.
  • Deeds that secure or release a debt.
  • Deeds into a trust, when the same transfer would be exempt if made straight to the beneficiaries. The register must be shown a signed statement saying so, and the signer keeps the supporting evidence for inspection by the Department of Revenue.
  • Deeds from a trustee to a trust beneficiary.
  • Deeds of distribution by a personal representative to heirs or devisees.
  • Deeds to a qualifying 501(c)(3) nonprofit, without actual consideration.

The statute also presumes that a deed transferring legal title or a beneficial interest is taxable unless the face of the deed or documentary proof shows an exemption. Form 521 has a line for the exemption number, so cite the right one when you file.

What a quitclaim deed cannot do

A quitclaim moves whatever title the grantor holds. It does not repair a clouded title. Three limits come up often.

First, the after-acquired title rule above. If the grantor owned half and later inherits the other half, the quitclaim holder does not automatically get it.

Second, recording priority. Under 76-238, a recorded instrument takes effect against creditors and later good-faith purchasers from the moment it is delivered to the register. An unrecorded one is void against a later buyer without notice who records first, though it stays valid between the two parties. In Schott v. Dosh (1896), a quitclaim holder was allowed to be a bona fide purchaser, so the deed type alone does not block that protection.

Third, timing. Section 76-237 treats a deed as recorded from the moment it is delivered to the register, in the order delivered. A deed signed in October but filed in spring leaves a gap in which a later recorded deed can win.

A quitclaim does not wipe out a mortgage, a judgment lien or a tax lien. If the house carries any of those, a title search shows what the grantee really receives.

Selling a house you received by quitclaim

A house that arrived by quitclaim deed sells like any other, but the buyer's title company will read the deed closely. Expect questions about whether an authorized officer took the acknowledgment, whether Form 521 was filed with the right exemption cited, and whether the grantor held full title to begin with.

The usual stories are a parent adding a child to title, a divorce moving a house to one spouse, or an heir signing over a share. All are legitimate. Trouble starts when the paperwork was informal and never recorded, or when a co-owner's signature is missing.

  • Pull the recorded deed from the county register of deeds and confirm the recording date and the book and page.
  • Check that every person who held title signed the deed.
  • Confirm whether any mortgage or judgment against the former owner is still of record.
  • Keep a copy of the filed Form 521 and any exemption statement.

Our team buys Nebraska houses as-is, including homes with messy paper trails. Title work decides how fast a sale closes, so the sooner you can show the recorded deed, the sooner we can talk through the numbers.

Frequently asked questions

Can I use a quitclaim deed to add someone to my Nebraska house title?

Yes. A quitclaim is a recordable deed under the definition in 76-203, so it can add a name. It needs an acknowledgment before an authorized officer, the proper page format and a Form 521 at the register of deeds. A deed to a spouse or child with no real consideration is on the stamp tax exemption list in 76-902.

How much does it cost to file a quitclaim deed in Nebraska?

The register of deeds charges $10 for the first page and $6 for each extra page under 33-109. A taxable deed also owes documentary stamp tax at $3.32 per $1,000 of value. Family transfers without consideration are exempt under 76-902.

Does the register of deeds check that a quitclaim deed is legally valid?

The register checks format and the transfer statement, not the underlying title. Under 76-214 the deed will not be recorded without a completed, signed Form 521, and the layout rules in 23-1503.01 apply. Whether the grantor really owned the property is a title question.

What happens if I never record my Nebraska quitclaim deed?

The deed stays valid between you and the person who signed it. Under 76-238, though, it is void against later good-faith purchasers and creditors who record first without notice. Recording promptly closes that gap.

Do I need a lawyer to prepare a Nebraska quitclaim deed?

The statutes do not require one, but the acknowledgment, format and tax rules are strict enough that mistakes are common. For anything beyond a simple, debt-free family transfer, ask a Nebraska real estate attorney or a title company to review it.

What a transfer on death deed does

A transfer on death deed names a beneficiary who gets the real estate when the owner dies. Until then the owner keeps full control of the house. The rules sit in the 76-34 series of Nebraska statutes, and 76-3410 governs the deed itself.

The deed must have the elements of an ordinary recordable deed, say that the transfer to the named beneficiary happens at the transferor's death, carry the statutory warnings, and be recorded in the proper county before the owner dies.

While the owner is alive, 76-3414 says the deed takes nothing away from anyone. The owner can still sell or mortgage the house. The beneficiary has no legal or equitable interest, and the beneficiary's own creditors cannot reach the property. The beneficiary does not need to be told, receive the deed, accept it or pay for it, because 76-3411 makes it effective without notice, delivery, acceptance or consideration.

The deed is also revocable, and 76-3406 says so even if the deed or another document claims otherwise.

Signing and witnessing

The transferor signs, or someone signs in the transferor's presence at his or her direction. At least two disinterested witnesses attest in writing, all before an officer who can administer oaths. That requirement is in 76-3409, which also supplies the form of the officer's certificate.

The sworn language in that form is specific. The transferor declares that he or she signs willingly, is eighteen or older, is of sound mind and is under no constraint or undue influence. The witnesses declare that they watched the transferor sign, in the transferor's presence and hearing, and that to the best of their knowledge those statements are true. The notary or other officer then certifies under official seal.

The witnesses carry real weight. A challenge based on missing disinterested witnesses must be filed within ninety days after the transferor's death, or after the last surviving transferor's death if there were several. After that, 76-3410(c) bars the claim.

Warnings the deed must contain

Every Nebraska transfer on death deed carries printed warnings, and deeds created after September 3, 2025 carry one more than older deeds. The text comes from 76-3410(b).

Warning topicWhat the deed must tell the owner
Inheritance taxThe property stays subject to Nebraska inheritance tax as if the transferor still owned it at death, and late payment carries interest and penalties
Beneficiary liabilityThe beneficiary can be personally liable, up to the value received, for Medicaid reimbursement, and possibly for estate claims, spousal and child allowances and administration costs
Medicaid eligibilityThe Department of Health and Human Services may require the deed to be revoked for the transferor or spouse to qualify or stay qualified
Insurance (deeds after Sept. 3, 2025)Property insurance may end thirty days after the owner's death unless the beneficiary is added to the policy or buys cover

A recorded deed is not invalidated because a warning is worded badly. The Medicaid point has its own statute, 76-3421, which confirms the department can require revocation. If long-term care is in the picture, ask an elder law attorney how this fits your plan before you record.

Recording the deed and what it costs

The deed goes to the register of deeds in the county where the property sits, and you have thirty days from the date of signing. It must also be recorded while the owner is alive. A deed signed and left in a drawer does nothing.

  • Recording fee. The usual register of deeds fee under 33-109 is $10 for the first page and $6 for each added page.
  • Stamp tax. None. 76-902 exempts transfer on death deeds and their revocations from the documentary stamp tax.
  • Transfer statement at filing. Not required when the deed itself is recorded, or for a revocation signed with the original formalities. 76-214 sets that out.
  • Page format. The usual layout rules still apply, including a blank three-inch strip at the top of the first page.

The transfer statement comes later, at the owner's death. 76-3412 requires a completed statement when the conveyance takes effect because of death. At that point 76-2,126 also calls for a death certificate to be filed with the register of deeds, with a cover sheet listing the document title, the earlier recording data, the grantor, the surviving grantee and the legal description.

What happens when the owner dies

The interest passes to the beneficiary named in the deed, subject to several rules in 76-3415 that surprise families.

  • Survival. The beneficiary must outlive the owner by one hundred twenty hours unless the deed sets a different period. A beneficiary who does not is treated as having died first.
  • Several beneficiaries. Unless the deed says otherwise, they take equal undivided shares with no right of survivorship. If one share fails for any reason, it goes to the others in proportion.
  • Existing debts. The beneficiary takes the property subject to all mortgages, liens, contracts and other interests that applied at death.
  • No title warranty. The property passes without covenant or warranty of title, even if the deed says otherwise.
  • Joint owners. If other joint owners survive the transferor, the property belongs to them by survivorship. The deed works only for the last surviving joint owner.
  • Divorce. A divorce, dissolution or annulment after recording revokes the disposition, as provided in section 30-2333.

A beneficiary may also refuse the gift in whole or in part by disclaimer under 76-3416, which points to section 30-2352.

Revoking or changing the deed

Revocation takes a recorded document. Tearing up the original or writing on it does not count, because 76-3413 says a recorded deed cannot be revoked by an act on the deed itself.

The statute allows four kinds of instrument:

  • a new transfer on death deed that revokes the earlier one expressly or by inconsistency;
  • a separate instrument of revocation, signed with the same witness and officer formalities as the original;
  • an ordinary deed made during life that revokes it expressly or by inconsistency;
  • an ordinary deed to a bona fide purchaser that does the same.

Most of these must be acknowledged after the deed being revoked and recorded before the owner dies, in the county where the first deed was recorded. A deed to a bona fide purchaser gets a longer window: it must be recorded by the later of thirty days after signing or the owner's death.

When there are several transferors, one transferor's revocation does not affect the others' interests. A deed from joint owners is revoked only if all living joint owners who signed it revoke.

Selling a house that has a transfer on death deed

While the owner is alive, the deed does not block a sale. The owner signs a normal deed to the buyer, and 76-3413 lists a deed to a bona fide purchaser as one way to revoke the earlier deed. Section 76-3414 confirms that the owner's right to transfer or encumber the property is untouched.

After the owner's death, a beneficiary who wants to sell usually needs the death certificate and cover sheet recorded first, so the county records show who now owns the home. Buyers and title companies look for those filings, the stamp tax exemption, and any liens that passed with the property.

Families in this spot often live out of state, and the house may be empty and need work. We buy Nebraska houses as-is, so repairs and clutter are no barrier to a conversation about selling.

Frequently asked questions

Does a Nebraska transfer on death deed avoid probate?

The deed passes the named real estate straight to the beneficiary at the owner's death, which is its purpose under the 76-34 series. It does not remove inheritance tax, and the beneficiary takes the property subject to existing liens under 76-3415.

Can I sell my house after signing a transfer on death deed?

Yes. Under 76-3414 the deed leaves the owner's right to transfer or encumber the property untouched during life. Section 76-3413 also lists a deed to a bona fide purchaser as a way to revoke it.

How many witnesses does a Nebraska transfer on death deed need?

Two or more disinterested witnesses, who sign along with the transferor before a notary or another officer authorized to administer oaths, under 76-3409.

Does a transfer on death deed pay Nebraska documentary stamp tax?

No. Section 76-902 exempts transfer on death deeds and their revocations. The normal recording fee of $10 for the first page and $6 for each added page still applies.

Can Medicaid affect a transfer on death deed in Nebraska?

Yes. The deed must warn that the Department of Health and Human Services may require revocation for Medicaid eligibility, and 76-3421 gives the department that power. The beneficiary can also be liable up to the value received for Medicaid reimbursement.

Nebraska and capital gains on a home sale

Nebraska does not run a special capital gains schedule. Individuals fall under four ordinary bracket rates, and whatever part of your home-sale profit escapes the federal exclusion simply flows into the Nebraska return and is taxed at those rates.

The top rate drops to 4.55% for tax year 2026 from 5.20% in 2025. Many websites still print the older figure, so confirm the current one before you estimate your bill.

Two income tax layers sit on a sale: federal rules set the taxable gain, then Nebraska's brackets apply to what remains. A third charge, the documentary stamp tax, is a fee for transferring the deed and is not an income tax, so it appears in its own section further down.

2026 Nebraska brackets

Starting with tax years that begin on January 1, 2026, Nebraska uses four brackets at 2.46%, 3.51%, 4.55% and 4.55%. The Department of Revenue sets dollar limits for each filing status.

Standard deductions for 2026 are $8,850 single and $17,700 joint. Last year's schedule had a 5.01% third bracket and a 5.20% top bracket, which means the year your sale closes changes the math. The state's rate chronology lists every earlier year.

How much gain the IRS lets you skip

If the house was your primary residence, federal income tax can often skip $250,000 of the profit, or $500,000 for spouses filing together. The IRS explains the rules in Topic 701 and Publication 523.

Two tests decide it. Ownership: you held title for 24 months inside the five-year window that ends on closing day. Use: you lived there for 24 months inside that window. The months need not match.

  • Married couples: one spouse satisfying the ownership test is enough, yet each spouse must satisfy the use test.
  • Took the exclusion on another house within the last two years? You generally cannot take it again.
  • Military, Foreign Service and intelligence community personnel on qualified extended duty can elect to pause the five-year window, up to 10 years.

Profit beyond the exclusion is what ends up on your returns, and it is taxed under both the federal and the Nebraska rates.

Federal rates on the taxable part

After a holding period over one year, federal net capital gain is taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%, depending on taxable income. IRS Topic 409 gives the thresholds, which move annually. Using 2025 figures, the 0% rate covers income to $48,350 for singles, $96,700 for joint filers and $64,750 for heads of household. The 15% rate then reaches $533,400, $600,050 and $566,700 respectively, and anything higher is taxed at 20%.

One year or less makes it a short-term gain, taxed as ordinary income. Depreciation you claimed during a rental period can push that slice to as much as 25%. Large investment income may also bring the net investment income tax (IRS Topic 559).

A loss brings no deduction. The IRS counts a loss on your own home as personal, so it cannot be claimed.

Owner lives out of state

Living elsewhere does not excuse you from a Nebraska return when you sell Nebraska property. Nebraska taxes nonresidents on Nebraska-source items, among them income, gain, loss and deductions that arise from owning or selling real property here.

People caught by this include:

  • Owners who left, rented the house, and then sold.
  • Heirs in other states who inherit a Nebraska house and sell.
  • Former residents who moved mid-year and sold in that same year and may be part-year residents.

The nonresident return is Form 1040N, and a Nonresident Income Tax Agreement form exists as well. Settle your filing status ahead of closing, either with the Department of Revenue or with a tax pro, since the sale may be your only Nebraska income that year.

Gain on an inherited house

Profit means the sale price minus adjusted basis. An inherited house gets its basis from special rules, not from the decedent's purchase price. Publication 551 deals with property received through gift or inheritance, and Topic 703 notes that improvements can add to basis.

An heir's profit, if any, turns on that figure. Keep proof of what the home was worth at death: an appraisal, estate inventory or county assessment record all work.

Nebraska inheritance tax is a different animal. It stands apart from income tax and is charged to whoever receives the property. Classes and rates are laid out in our Nebraska estate and inheritance tax guide.

Documentary stamp tax

The seller carries the documentary stamp tax, due when the deed is recorded. Value is counted in $1,000 units, with any leftover fraction rounded up to a full unit, at $3.32 a unit for deeds recorded July 18, 2026 or later. Before then the unit price was $2.32. The register of deeds in the county takes payment.

Recording also needs a completed Real Estate Transfer Statement, Form 521, submitted by the buyer or the buyer's agent (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-214). Some transfers carry no stamp tax:

  • Deeds between spouses or parent and child where nothing real is paid.
  • Distribution deeds from a personal representative to heirs or devisees.
  • Transfer on death deeds.
  • Foreclosure-avoidance deeds that secure or release a debt.

A normal sale to an unrelated buyer gets no exemption. Request the dollar figure from your title company ahead of time.

Paperwork after the sale

Received a Form 1099-S? Then the sale goes on your return, even if the gain is fully excludable, and it goes there too if only part of the gain is excludable. Use Form 8949 and Schedule D.

Taxable profit can also trigger quarterly estimated payments, which Publication 505 covers. A spring closing followed by a settle-up the next April risks an underpayment penalty, so ask your preparer about paying before year end.

If the buyer pays you over several years under an installment contract, you generally use the installment method unless you elect out. The home sale exclusion remains available in that setup.

Seller tax checklist

  • Note your purchase date and price, and collect every improvement receipt.
  • Verify 24 of the last 60 months as your residence.
  • Compare the 2026 and 2025 Nebraska schedules if rate changes touch your closing year.
  • Ask whether an heir or out-of-state owner must file in Nebraska.
  • Work the $3.32 per $1,000 stamp tax into closing costs for deeds recorded from July 18, 2026.
  • Hand your preparer the 1099-S and the settlement statement together.

This is not tax advice, and a Nebraska CPA or enrolled agent can run your own numbers. A house in rough shape can still sell: Cash Home Buyers makes as-is cash offers, so you can plan the tax side before you commit.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Nebraska capital gains tax rate for 2026?

There is no separate rate. Taxable gain runs through the individual brackets, which are 2.46%, 3.51%, 4.55% and 4.55% for 2026.

Do I owe Nebraska tax if I sell my main home?

Only if gain is left after the federal exclusion of up to $250,000, or $500,000 for a joint return. Excluded gain stays out of income, though a Form 1099-S still means you report the sale.

How long must I live in the house to use the exclusion?

Own it and live in it for at least 24 months each during the five years before you sell. The two 24-month periods can fall at different times.

Does Nebraska tax a nonresident who sells a house in the state?

Yes. Income and gain tied to Nebraska real property are taxable for nonresidents, who file Form 1040N.

Who pays the Nebraska documentary stamp tax?

The seller, as grantor, pays when the deed is recorded with the register of deeds. For deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026 the rate is $3.32 per $1,000 of value.

How Nebraska probate works

Probate is a county court case that places a dead person's assets and debts under court supervision. It exists to protect heirs from fraud and embezzlement, to make sure estate taxes are paid, and to make sure creditors are paid. The case begins when a will is admitted to formal or informal probate.

Nebraska county courts handle the lawful distribution of what a person owned and owed as an estate. The person who runs it is the personal representative, and that is the person who signs the deed if the house is sold.

A family hoping to sell an inherited house needs answers to three questions: who has authority, whether a court appointment is needed at all, and how long creditors have to come forward. Each has a statute behind it, covered below.

Who can be personal representative

Section 30-2412 sets an order of priority, and the court follows it in formal and informal proceedings alike. A person nominated in a probated will comes first. After that the order runs:

  1. The surviving spouse, if the spouse is also a devisee under the will.
  2. Other devisees.
  3. The surviving spouse, even if not a devisee.
  4. Other heirs.
  5. Any creditor, but only forty-five days or more after the death.

Nobody under age nineteen can serve, and in a formal proceeding the court can turn down a person it finds unsuitable. Someone with priority may nominate another qualified person to act. Only formal proceedings allow objections to an appointment.

Much of the friction over an inherited house starts with this list. Two siblings with equal priority must agree, among those who do not renounce, on who acts for them. Until somebody is appointed, nobody can sign a deed for the estate.

What the representative can do with the house

Under section 30-2476, a personal representative acting reasonably for the benefit of the interested persons may dispose of an estate asset, land included, for cash or on credit, at public or private sale. A will or court order can restrict that authority. The same section covers several steps useful for a house in poor shape:

  • Making ordinary or extraordinary repairs, and demolishing or building improvements.
  • Leasing the property for a term that can outlast the administration.
  • Abandoning property the representative considers valueless, or so encumbered or run down that it brings the estate no benefit.
  • Selling, mortgaging or leasing real or personal property for cash, on credit, or both.

Section 30-2472 gives the representative the same power over title as an absolute owner, usable without notice, hearing or court order unless the court directs otherwise. So a will that does not restrict sales may allow a sale to move forward with no hearing, while a will requiring court approval changes that.

When a relative or the representative wants to buy

Any interested person can undo a sale to the personal representative, the representative's spouse, agent or attorney, or a company in which the representative holds a substantial interest. Section 30-2474 calls it voidable, and the rule reaches any transaction tainted by a substantial conflict of interest.

Two exceptions apply. The sale stands if the will or a contract the decedent made expressly authorized it, or if the court approved it after notice to the interested persons. A person who consented after fair disclosure cannot complain later.

Families run into this when one heir wants to keep the house and buy out the rest. Put the approval on the record, or have every heir sign a written consent after full disclosure. A buyer dealing at arm's length raises no such issue, one reason estates often sell to outsiders.

Creditor claims and the timeline

Creditors get a short window in Nebraska, and the clock runs from a published notice. Under section 30-2483, once a personal representative is appointed the clerk publishes a notice once a week for three weeks in a newspaper of general circulation in the county. Claims must be presented within two months after first publication or they are barred. First publication must happen within thirty days after the appointment.

Type of claimDeadline
Claim that arose before death, notice properly givenTwo months after first publication
Same, but notice was not properly givenThree years after death
Claim arising at or after deathFour months after it arises
Late creditor asking for more timeApply within sixty days after the deadline; court may add up to thirty days

Mortgages, pledges and other liens survive these deadlines. Section 30-2485(c) leaves room for a proceeding to enforce a lien on estate property.

If the decedent was 55 or older, or lived in a medical institution as defined in section 68-919, the notice must also go to the Department of Health and Human Services with the decedent's Social Security number. A notice that skips the department's delivery requirements is void. Raise this step with the estate attorney early, since it affects when the estate can close.

Skipping probate with a small estate affidavit

Nebraska has an affidavit route for small estates. The whole estate, less liens and encumbrances, must be worth $100,000 or less. At least thirty days must have gone by since the death, and you cannot be a creditor of the estate. No personal representative, application or petition for one may be pending.

Separate affidavit forms exist for personal property and for real property, along with a Probate Inventory Worksheet, an inheritance tax form and a title transfer form for a deceased person's vehicle.

The real property affidavit goes to the register of deeds and uses the value on the assessment rolls, less taxes due (section 30-24,129). Because that value comes from the rolls and not from a sale price, a modest house can fit under the limit on paper.

For a house worth more, or when heirs disagree, formal or informal probate is the likelier path. Transfer on death deeds sit outside probate, but they must be recorded before the owner dies.

Before heirs sell an inherited house

First find out whether anyone has legal authority to sign. An heir who has not been appointed cannot convey a house that belongs to an estate, and the buyer's title company will ask for proof of who has authority.

This short checklist keeps a sale moving:

  • Get a certified death certificate and locate the original will.
  • Ask the county court clerk whether a case has been opened and who was appointed.
  • Learn the mortgage balance, tax status and any liens before you set a price.
  • Insure and secure the house while the estate is open.
  • Decide whether the creditor claim period must run before proceeds are distributed.

A buyer who purchases as is, such as Cash Home Buyers, can cut out the repair and showing steps, though the probate rules stay the same. The deed still comes from the personal representative, and the proceeds still go through the estate. This page is general information, not legal advice.

Frequently asked questions

How long does Nebraska probate take?

There is no fixed length. When notice is properly given, the creditor window runs two months after first publication, so even a simple estate cannot close before then. Disputes, tax issues and lien problems add time.

Do I need a lawyer for a Nebraska estate?

The courts offer self-help instructions and forms, and small estates can use affidavits. A formal case with disputes, or one involving a house sale, often benefits from an attorney, because the forms may not fit every case.

Can I sell the house before probate is finished?

Yes, if a personal representative has been appointed and the will or a court order does not restrict a sale. Section 30-2476 lets the representative sell land at public or private sale. Without an appointment, no one has authority to sign for the estate.

What if I am a creditor of the person who died?

A creditor may serve as personal representative only forty-five days or more after the death, and only after those with higher priority. A creditor also cannot use the small estate affidavit.

What if the notice to creditors was never published?

Claims that arose before death can then be presented for up to three years after the death under section 30-2485(a)(2). Confirm that notice ran before you distribute money to heirs.

Where to record a deed in Nebraska

Recording happens at the county level. Take the deed to the register of deeds for the county that holds the land. Nebraska keeps no central deed index, so an Omaha house and a western farmhouse are filed in two unrelated offices. Statutes such as 33-109 name both the register of deeds and the county clerk, because in some counties the clerk does the register's job.

Offices differ in how they work. In Douglas County, the Assessor and Register of Deeds share an office at 1819 Farnam Street, 4th Floor, Omaha, and checks are made out to the Douglas County Assessor/Register of Deeds. Visa, Mastercard, American Express and Discover are accepted there. Smaller counties are plainer. Chase County lists a post office box and a brief fee schedule, and Nemaha County simply restates the state fees and stamp tax.

Before you travel or mail anything, call the county office. Ask which payment types it takes, whether e-recording is offered, and whether it wants the original or will accept a copy. Those practices are local, and the statutes leave them to each office.

What to bring to the recording office

Bring the signed and acknowledged deed, a completed Real Estate Transfer Statement, and payment for the recording fee and any stamp tax. The usual cause of a rejected deed is a missing transfer statement. 76-214 forbids the register to record without one.

Bring thisWhat to know
Signed, acknowledged deedIn Nebraska the acknowledgment is taken by a judge or court clerk, a U.S. magistrate or a notary, inside that officer's jurisdiction (76-217)
Form 521Signed by the grantee or an authorized agent, with items 1 through 27 completed (76-214)
Recording fee$10 for the first page, $6 for each added page (33-109)
Documentary stamp tax$3.32 per $1,000 of value, unless an exemption applies (76-901)
Page layout3 by 8.5 inch blank space at the top of page one; paper from 8.5 by 11 to 8.5 by 14 inches (23-1503.01)

Preparing the document

The page has to be built so the register can stamp and copy it. 23-1503.01 spells out the details.

  • Keep the top three inches of page one empty, edge to edge. Skip that and the office may insert a page, or use a page's back, and bill you the page fee.
  • Use white paper, twenty-pound weight or heavier, with black print and no watermarks. E-filed copies follow the same black-on-white rule.
  • Choose readable type. Eight points or larger is presumed readable.
  • Ink signatures should be black or dark blue. Digital or electronic signatures are accepted.
  • Put each party's printed or stamped name beneath the signature, and make sure no stamp covers other text.
  • Never tape or attach anything over printed information on the instrument.

Some categories are exempt from these rules, including instruments signed before August 27, 2011, documents executed outside the United States, certified government copies, and instruments formatted for court requirements. If your deed fits one of those groups, ask the register which rules still apply.

What happens after recording

Once the deed is recorded, the register writes the book and page on Form 521 and hands the form to the county assessor. The assessor processes it under instructions from the state's Property Tax Administrator and sends it on to the Tax Commissioner. When the deed is recorded the register completes items 28 through 30, forwards the original to the assessor and keeps a copy. The chain is set out in 76-214.

Anyone can view these statements at the Tax Commissioner's, assessor's or register's office until the record is disposed of under the retention schedule. So the price and deed type you write on the form can show up later in an appraiser's or a neighbor's research.

The form also asks whether an affidavit under 76-2,141 is needed. That applies to property in a county or area with an active air force ballistic missile field. Read the form instructions for that line if your county might be affected.

Why the recording date matters

Under 76-237, deeds are recorded in the order delivered, and a deed counts as recorded from the time it reaches the register. Section 76-238 supplies the consequence. Once recorded, an instrument beats creditors and later good-faith buyers as of delivery. An unrecorded one loses to a later buyer who had no notice and records first, yet it still binds the people who signed it.

For a seller this is practical. If a sale closes and the buyer's deed sits unrecorded for weeks, a creditor's claim against the seller could be recorded first. Filing promptly after closing shortens that window.

Transfer on death deeds have their own deadline. They must be recorded within thirty days of signing and before the owner's death. That rule is in 76-3410 and is covered in our guide to those deeds.

Copies, no-fee filings and death certificates

Beyond the standard fee, counties charge for copies, and a few filings follow their own rules.

  • Certified copies. $1.50 per page under 33-109. Chase County adds that certification is charged on top of the ordinary photocopy fee.
  • Plain copies. Douglas County charges $5.00 per document for requests of more than ten.
  • No-fee documents. Federal and state tax liens are recorded without a fee, but only when they come from the Nebraska Secretary of State.
  • Death certificates. If title moves through a transfer on death deed, joint tenancy or the end of a life estate, 76-2,126 calls for a death certificate on file with the register of deeds. A transfer on death deed also needs a cover sheet that names the recorded document, the grantor, the surviving grantee and the legal description.
  • Fee earmark. $2.50 of each first-page fee and 50 cents of each added page go to records preservation and technology.

Fees can change whenever the statute does. Call the county before writing your check.

Recording a deed when you sell

A title or escrow company often prepares the transfer statement and files the deed at a sale, although no statute demands that. If you are handling a family transfer or private sale yourself, those jobs are yours.

If an old unrecorded deed sits behind your house, record it first. Lenders and buyers search the register's index, and any hole in the chain delays things. Gather what you have, confirm each paper is of record, close the gap, and then pick a closing date. Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a deed in Nebraska?

Go to the register of deeds in the property's county. Where one office does both jobs, that is the county clerk. In Douglas County, recordings are taken at 1819 Farnam Street in Omaha.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Nebraska?

Under 33-109 you pay $10 on page one and $6 on every page after it. Unless 76-902 exempts the deed, add documentary stamp tax of $3.32 per $1,000 of value.

Can the register of deeds refuse to record my deed?

Yes. Under 76-214 the register shall not record a deed if the grantee has not furnished the completed transfer statement. A deed without the required blank space may be accepted only with an added page and fee under 23-1503.01.

Is a deed valid if I do not record it?

Yes, as between the people who signed it. Against a later purchaser or creditor who records first without notice, 76-238 makes it void. Recording is how the new owner stays safe.

Can I get a certified copy of my recorded deed?

Yes. Certification costs $1.50 a page under 33-109, and the office may add its own photocopy fee. Have the book and page ready, or ask them to search by owner name.
